name: Horizontal stripes and layering for width

lead: People wear horizontal stripes and stacked layers to make the chest and shoulders look wider and the upper body bulkier, with the effect visible as soon as the outfit is on.

Layers add real fabric volume around the torso, and horizontal patterns are said to lead the eye sideways across the body. No direct studies of stripes or layering on perceived body width were found; related illusion research uses line drawings, not clothing.

paras: People choose horizontally striped tops, thicker knits, and layered shirts, tees and jackets, often on slimmer frames wanting more upper-body presence. The effect is immediate and works with any wardrobe.
No health risks apply. Heavy layering can add bulk at the waist as well as the chest, and in hot weather it can be uncomfortable.

angle.text: People wear horizontal stripes and layers to look broader across the chest and shoulders; layers add real volume and stripes are said to draw the eye sideways. The effect is immediate with clothing alone. No direct studies were found.

lead: Horizontal stripes and layering are clothing techniques that people in looksmaxxing and style communities use to make a slim upper body look broader or bulkier. Layering, for example a jacket over a sweater over a shirt, adds actual fabric volume around the shoulders, chest and arms, and horizontal patterns are said to draw the eye sideways across the torso, so the frame reads as wider.

The perception research on stripes is distinct from the claim. In a 2011 i-Perception paper, Peter Thompson and Kyriaki Mikellidou found that horizontally striped shapes were judged taller and narrower than vertically striped ones of equal size: a vertically striped rectangle had to be extended 7.1 percent vertically to match a horizontally striped square, and a horizontally striped rectangle had to be 4.5 percent wider to match a vertically striped square. [1] This is the Helmholtz illusion, named for the nineteenth-century scientist Hermann von Helmholtz, and the authors reported that it also held for a line drawing of a woman and stereoscopic photos of a half-body mannequin. [1]

A 2013 follow-up by Hiroshi Ashida and colleagues reported that the effect varied between viewers and depended on the body shape shown, being stronger for thin figures than fat ones and possibly reversing for the latter, and that results were influenced by the order in which figures were presented. [2] These studies describe how striped shapes are perceived; they do not report horizontal stripes widening a body, while layered clothing adds physical bulk.

paras: Practitioners describe two ideas. One is that horizontal stripes make a torso read as wider. The other is that layering adds bulk where the wearer is slim. Common layered combinations include jackets over knitwear over shirts, overshirts, and thicker fabrics at the shoulder and chest. No source examined documents when either idea entered looksmaxxing culture.

The Helmholtz illusion is the effect in which a square filled with horizontal lines is judged to be taller and narrower than an otherwise identical square filled with vertical lines. [1] Thompson and Mikellidou's paper, titled for the claim that horizontal stripes will not make a person look fatter, tested it with striped shapes, a line drawing of a woman, stereoscopic photos of a mannequin and a three-dimensional cylinder, and reported no support for horizontal lines being fattening. [1]

Ashida, Kuraguchi and Miyoshi reported that horizontally striped squares looked thinner, that the effect was stronger for thin figures and may have reversed for fat ones, and that participants differed widely, suggesting that what a viewer attends to matters. [2] A separate 2022 paper in the same journal described a common belief about striped clothing and body shape in an 1813 Japanese beauty handbook, showing the question long predates online communities. [3]

The vertical-horizontal illusion, in which a vertical line is overestimated in length relative to an equal horizontal line, persists even when observers know the lines match. It has been studied with simple line figures, and it is a separate effect from the Helmholtz illusion. [4]
No clinical studies found. Laboratory perception studies of striped shapes and figures are described above. [1][2]

timeline.event: A Japanese beauty handbook records a belief about striped clothing and perceived body shape. [3]
